slides.title: Steps Check
slides.question: According to the guide, how many main points can you reasonably convey in a 20–30 minute talk?

options.explanation: The guide says 2-3 main points only.
Step 3 says: 'you can reasonably convey only 2-3 main points in a 20- or 30-minute talk.'

options.text: As many as you can fit
options.explanation: The guide emphasizes less is more.

slides.title: Pointers for Giving the Best Talk
Delivery Quiz
slides.question: What should you NOT do according to the tips for giving a scientific presentation?

options.text: Maintain eye contact with the audience
Read your talk word for word from notes
options.explanation: The guide explicitly says 'Do not read your talk!' — talk directly to people as you would in conversation.
The guide says 'Be enthusiastic! If you don't act excited by your results, don't expect the audience to be!'

options.text: Thank the audience at the end
options.explanation: The guide says to thank the audience.

lessons.title: Key Terms
lessons.description: Vocabulary from Tips for Scientific Presentations.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: The systematic process or set of methods used in scientific research or presentations
slides.context: Used to describe the structured approach to presenting scientific work.
slides.example: Step 4: Create an outline of your talk — this will build in the logical organization of your methodology.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: A reference to a published work used to support ideas or acknowledge the source of information
slides.context: Required on the title slide for journal club presentations.
slides.example: Title Slide: Your names and affiliations, paper citation (for JC), venue and date.

slides.title: Word Card
slides.translation: A scientific presentation gathering where members present and discuss published research papers
slides.context: A specific type of scientific presentation where critique and citation summary are required.
slides.example: Journal club presentations require a critique slide — what was wrong with/good about the paper?
